questions.prompt: A non-inverting amplifier with ideal gain 25 (\(f=0.04\)) uses an op-amp with \(A=4000\). What is its static gain error, in percent?
questions.explanation:
\(T=Af=160\), and the error is \(1/(1+T)=1/161=0.62\%\). The gain is 24.84 instead of 25.
• \(1/A=0.025\%\) ignores f; the error depends on the loop gain, not the open-loop gain alone.
• 4% is f itself.

questions.prompt: Two amplifiers use the same op-amp (\(A=10^4\)). One has ideal gain 2 and the other has ideal gain 200. Which has the larger static gain error, and why?
options: Both are the same, since they use the same op-amp
The gain-200 amplifier: its feedback factor is 100 times smaller, so its loop gain \(T=A/200=50\) is much less than \(A/2=5000\)
The gain-2 amplifier, because it feeds back more of the output
Neither has any error, since \(A\) is large
questions.explanation:
The error is \(1/(1+T)\) with \(T=Af\), and \(f=1/G_{ideal}\). High closed-loop gain means little feedback and a small loop gain: 2% error for the gain-200 design versus 0.02% for the gain-2 design. This is the core trade-off of feedback amplifiers.
• Same op-amp does not mean same loop gain.
• More feedback reduces the error rather than increasing it.
• 'A is large' is relative: \(A/200\) is only 50.

questions.prompt: You need a gain-of-50 non-inverting amplifier with at most 0.1% static gain error. What is the minimum op-amp open-loop gain A?
questions.explanation:
Require \(1/(1+T)\le0.001\Rightarrow T\ge999\). With \(f=1/50\): \(A\ge999\times50=4.995\times10^4\).
• 999 is the required loop gain, not A.
• \(5\times10^4\) is the rounded version (\(T\approx1000\)).
• \(1000/50=20\) divides by the gain instead of multiplying.

questions.prompt: An op-amp with \(A(jf)=\dfrac{2\times10^5}{1+jf/5\ \mathrm{Hz}}\) is used in a gain-of-10 amplifier (\(f=0.1\)). For a 20 kHz signal, what is the error ratio \(\left|\dfrac{1}{1+T}\right|\) in percent?
questions.explanation:
At 20 kHz: \(|A|\approx2\times10^5\cdot5/20000=50\), with phase near \(-90^\circ\). So \(T\approx-j5\) and \(|1+T|=|1-j5|=5.10\), giving an error ratio of 19.6%. The DC loop gain is \(2\times10^4\), but at 20 kHz only about 5 is left.
• 0.005% uses the DC loop gain.
• \(1/6=16.7\%\) adds \(|T|\) to 1 as if they were in phase.
questions.figure_alt: Open-loop gain of the op-amp: 106 dB to 5 Hz, then falling 20 dB per decade.

questions.prompt: For the same amplifier at 20 kHz (\(T\approx-j5\)), what is the closed-loop gain MAGNITUDE \(\dfrac1f\left|\dfrac{T}{1+T}\right|\)?
questions.explanation:
\(\left|\dfrac{T}{1+T}\right|=\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{1+25}}=0.981\), so the gain is \(9.81\), only 1.9% low, even though the error ratio is about 20%. The missing part of the error shows up mostly as phase: \(\angle\dfrac{T}{1+T}\approx-11^\circ\).
• \(10(1-0.196)=8.04\) subtracts the error ratio from the magnitude, but the error is in quadrature.
• 10 ignores the finite loop gain.

questions.prompt: A unity-gain buffer (\(f=1\)) uses an op-amp with \(A_0=10^5\). What is its static gain error?
options: About 1%
Exactly zero, because the gain is 1
About 10 ppm (0.001%): \(T=A_0\) is as large as it can be, because the buffer feeds back the whole output
About 50%, because the input and output are tied together
questions.explanation:
With \(f=1\), \(T=A_0=10^5\) and the error is \(1/(1+10^5)\approx10\ \mathrm{ppm}\). The follower has the largest loop gain of any configuration, which makes it the most accurate. As a later skill shows, it is also the hardest to keep stable.
• 1% would need \(T\approx100\).
• A gain of 1 still has a small shortfall: \(A/(1+A)\).
• Tying output to input is the feedback, not a short circuit.

questions.prompt: An op-amp is modeled as a pure integrator \(A=\omega_u/(j\omega)\) (infinite DC gain), with \(f_u=1\ \mathrm{MHz}\) and \(f=0.1\). Which describes its errors?
options: Zero error at every frequency, since the gain is infinite
A static error of 10%, constant with frequency
Zero static error, but a dynamic error of about \(|1/(1+T)|\approx10\%\) at 10 kHz, where \(|T|\approx10\)
Infinite error at DC
questions.explanation:
\(T=Af=\dfrac{f\,\omega_u}{j\omega}\): infinite at DC, so the static error \(1/(1+T_0)\) is 0. At 10 kHz, \(|T|=0.1\times10^6/10^4=10\) and \(|1/(1+T)|=1/|1-j10|\approx9.95\%\).
'Infinite gain' only at DC: the trap is equating infinite DC gain with perfect accuracy at all frequencies.

questions.prompt: A gain-of-5 amplifier uses an op-amp with a gain-bandwidth product of 10 MHz, so its closed-loop response is a single pole at 2 MHz. How long does a small step take to settle within 0.1% of its final value, in ns?
questions.explanation:
\(\tau=1/(2\pi\cdot2\ \mathrm{MHz})=79.6\ \mathrm{ns}\). Settling to 0.1% needs \(e^{-t/\tau}=10^{-3}\), so \(t=\tau\ln1000=6.91\tau=550\ \mathrm{ns}\).
• 79.6 ns is a single time constant (63%).
• Using the 10 MHz GBW for the pole gives 110 ns: the closed-loop bandwidth is GBW divided by the gain.
• \(\tau\ln100=367\ \mathrm{ns}\) is the 1% settling time.
questions.figure_alt: Single-pole closed-loop step response rising exponentially to its final value.

questions.prompt: A feedback amplifier's closed-loop response is a single pole at \(f_c\). At \(f=f_c/10\), how do its magnitude and phase errors compare?
options: Both are about 10%
The magnitude is 10% low and the phase is exact
Both are negligible, under 0.01%
The magnitude is only about 0.5% low, but the phase lags by about 5.7°
questions.explanation:
\(|1/(1+j0.1)|=1/\sqrt{1.01}=0.995\), a 0.5% error, but \(\angle=-\tan^{-1}0.1=-5.7^\circ\). Magnitude error grows as the square of \(f/f_c\), while phase error grows linearly. Systems that care about timing (feedback loops, multi-channel measurements) feel the phase error first.
• The 10% figure is the ratio \(f/f_c\), not either error.
• The phase is far from exact.
• 5.7° is not negligible in most loops.

questions.prompt: Preview of the source follower. Later you will see a transistor follower whose voltage gain has the form \(\dfrac{T}{1+T}\), i.e. a feedback loop with \(f=1\) and loop gain \(T\). If \(T=9\), what is its gain?
questions.explanation: \(\dfrac{T}{1+T}=\dfrac{9}{10}=0.9\). With \(f=1\) the ideal gain is 1, and the static error \(1/(1+T)=10\%\) explains why such followers have gain a bit below 1. More loop gain gives a better follower.

questions.prompt: Preview of source degeneration (local feedback). A stage has forward gain \(G=50\) and feedback that makes \(T=4\), so its gain is \(G/(1+T)=10\). The device's \(G\) increases by 2% (to 51, with \(f\) unchanged). By what percent does the closed-loop gain change?
questions.explanation:
\(f=T/G=0.08\). New gain \(=\dfrac{51}{1+51\times0.08}=\dfrac{51}{5.08}=10.039\), a change of \(0.394\%\).
Sensitivity is reduced by \(1+T=5\): \(2\%/5=0.4\%\). Degeneration in transistor amplifiers uses exactly this trade (gain for stability against device variation).

questions.prompt: Preview of transistor amplifiers. A transistor gain stage has a voltage gain that varies by \(\pm30\%\) with temperature and manufacturing. You need a gain accurate to \(\pm0.3\%\). Using only ideas from feedback errors, what works?
options: Use the stage open-loop and select parts carefully
Make a stage with about \(100\times\) more gain than needed and close a loop with a precise \(f\), so \(T\approx100\) divides the variation by \(\sim100\)
Close a loop with \(T\approx1\)
Add a second identical stage in series to average the errors
questions.explanation: Closed-loop sensitivity is the open-loop sensitivity divided by \(1+T\): \(30\%/101\approx0.3\%\). That requires excess forward gain (\(G=T/f\)) which is then 'spent' on accuracy. A cascade without feedback multiplies variations instead of averaging them; \(T\approx1\) only halves them.
